title: The Gang Gets Whacked (1)

jokes.text: Mac suggests wiping a rusty circuit breaker with a wet rag, then proposes jamming it with a screwdriver because the rubber handle will 'ground' him
jokes.setup: Mac and Dennis are trying to fix a dangerous circuit breaker and debating safety measures
jokes.punchline: Mac's understanding of electrical safety is completely wrong yet delivered with total confidence — rubber handle grounds you, standing on rubber keeps you safe, etc.
jokes.explanation: Classic Mac idiocy: he's confidently wrong about science in a way that escalates. The character integration is strong because Mac's blustering pseudo-expertise is a core trait. Runs a little long but sets the episode's tone of incompetence.

jokes.text: Mac proposes jumping into midair to touch a live wire so you won't get electrocuted — but warns you'll be 'blown to bits' when you land still holding it
jokes.setup: The gang is debating how to safely touch live wires
jokes.punchline: Mac's solution is to leap into the air mid-fix — granting temporary safety — only to be destroyed upon landing, as if that's a preferable outcome
jokes.explanation: The internal logic is beautifully broken — Mac acknowledges the problem is solved mid-air only to create a worse problem on landing, delivered as genuine problem-solving. Strong character integration and genuinely surprising comedic premise.

jokes.text: Mac cites Tango and Cash as his source for electrical safety science
jokes.setup: Mac has been confidently explaining how electricity works
jokes.punchline: His entire worldview is sourced from an 80s action movie — 'I saw it in Tango and Cash'
jokes.explanation: Perfect economy — one line completely reframes everything Mac has said. Specific movie choice (Tango and Cash, not Die Hard) is funnier and more authentic to Mac's character. High quotability.

jokes.text: Dennis says Mac will need a harness because he'll have to be 'swinging in the air' to fix the breaker — accepting Mac's insane logic
jokes.setup: Mac's Tango and Cash theory has been dismissed
jokes.punchline: Dennis pivots to fully endorsing the jumping-in-the-air solution, requesting a harness for mid-air electrical work
jokes.explanation: A satisfying button on the opening bit — Dennis rejecting Mac's theory only to circle back and endorse the worst part of it. The callback lands but isn't exceptional.

jokes.text: Mac arrives with speakers he found 'off the back of a truck' instead of the flashlights he was sent to get, celebrates gleefully while there's no electricity to power them
jokes.setup: The bar has no electricity; Mac was sent to get flashlights
jokes.punchline: He returns with electric speakers, bragging about the score, oblivious that they need electricity — the very thing they're missing — to use them
jokes.explanation: Well-structured irony — Mac's idiocy is self-defeating in the most direct possible way. 'We don't have any electricity!' is the perfect deflating punchline. Good situational comedy.

jokes.text: Opening a speaker crate reveals 'a big bag of drugs' — Charlie's flat, matter-of-fact delivery
jokes.setup: Mac has excitedly brought contraband speakers to a powerless bar
jokes.punchline: Inside the crate: a massive bag of drugs. Charlie's response — 'That's a... big bag of drugs' — is perfectly flat and understated
jokes.explanation: The deadpan understatement does a lot of work. 'That's a... big bag of drugs' is the funniest possible response — not panic, not excitement, just quiet acknowledgment. Economy score is high because it achieves maximum effect in six words.

jokes.text: Mac's response to finding mob drugs: 'Relax, dude. They're gonna be shit out of luck 'cause no one saw us take the speakers. Did they?' — said with complete confidence
jokes.setup: Charlie warns that someone is going to be looking for the drugs in the speakers
jokes.punchline: Mac confidently declares no one saw them, treating this as a solved problem — when of course they absolutely were seen, as we learn moments later
jokes.explanation: Classic Mac overconfidence that the audience knows is wrong. Gets rewatch value because on rewatch you know the gangsters were watching. Functional dramatic irony.

jokes.text: The gang methodically eliminates every option for disposing of the drugs — trash (kids), burning (fumes), burying (kids with shovels), police — in a roundabout committee discussion
jokes.setup: The gang agrees the drugs are bad news and must go
jokes.punchline: Every reasonable disposal option is shot down with absurd but internally logical reasoning, delivered as a serious policy debate
jokes.explanation: The 'fume situation' and 'kids running with shovels' reasoning is funny in its pseudo-logic, but the sequence runs a bit long without a killer punchline. Functions as connective tissue more than a standout joke.

jokes.text: Charlie interprets 'sell the drugs to fix the bar' as 'do the drugs and then try to fix all the lights'
jokes.setup: Dennis is explaining the plan to flip the drugs for money to fix the electricity
jokes.punchline: Charlie has heard: take the drugs, then attempt electrical work while high
jokes.explanation: Perfectly in character for Charlie — his misunderstanding isn't random, it's exactly the wrong conclusion that makes complete internal sense to Charlie's chaotic brain. 'That's asinine' from Dennis is the ideal reaction beat. High character integration because only Charlie arrives at this specific wrong answer.

jokes.text: Frank enters calling them 'scumbags' and declares 'Back in my day, only the biggest pieces of shit dealt drugs'
jokes.setup: The gang is debating drug-dealing plans
jokes.punchline: Frank — a cartoonishly corrupt man — lectures them on moral standards with total sincerity, as if he occupies the moral high ground
jokes.explanation: The irony of Frank — a man who will shortly suggest prostitution as a business plan — lecturing on drug-dealing ethics is rich. 'Biggest pieces of shit' is a great line. Character integration is high because only Frank delivers this hypocrisy with complete conviction.

jokes.text: Mac says 'I don't think you can call dibs on a shady people-smuggler'
jokes.setup: Frank is upset that the gang wants to use his criminal contact Bingo
jokes.punchline: Mac applies the logic of normal social etiquette (calling dibs) to organized crime contacts
jokes.explanation: Economical and sharp — the collision of mundane social rules with criminal underworld logic in one crisp sentence. 'You can't call dibs on a people-smuggler' is quotable and punchy.

jokes.text: Mac promises not to mention Frank's name — immediately cuts to Bingo meeting where Mac says 'Hey, Bingo. Frank sent us.' Frank is told: 'I'm gonna skin that son of a bitch and wear his face.'
jokes.setup: Frank desperately pleads 'just do not mention my name!' The gang assures him they won't
jokes.punchline: Hard cut to Mac immediately announcing Frank's name — first thing out of his mouth — followed by a viscerally violent threat
jokes.explanation: Near-perfect comedic structure. The setup is clear, the promise is sincere (or at least stated), and the betrayal is IMMEDIATE — no delay, no hesitation. 'Frank sent us' is the first thing Mac says. Then the threat escalates beautifully to skin-wearing. The economy is exceptional: two lines of setup, two words of punchline. This is very close to the 8.0 anchor in quality.

jokes.text: Bingo's response to hearing Frank's name: 'Frank, huh? I'm gonna skin that son of a bitch and wear his face.'
jokes.setup: Dennis has just said 'Frank sent us' to their shady contact Bingo
jokes.punchline: Bingo's calm, specific threat to skin Frank and wear his face — delivered with the matter-of-fact tone of someone saying 'Oh, I know Frank'
jokes.explanation: The specificity of 'skin that son of a bitch and wear his face' — delivered as a casual response rather than a dramatic threat — is what makes this land. The tone does the heavy lifting. It's maximally quotable and perfectly dark. High rewatch value because you appreciate the calm delivery more each time.

jokes.text: Bingo tells Mac and Charlie not to look at him, then makes them look up — 'Is this good?' 'That's fine. Now speak.'
jokes.setup: Mac and Charlie enter to meet dangerous drug dealer Bingo
jokes.punchline: Bingo has an inexplicable eye-contact ritual — look up, freeze, now speak — delivered as if it's completely normal criminal etiquette
jokes.explanation: A great character quirk for Bingo — the power dynamic is established through bizarre ritual rather than explicit threat. The compliance of Mac and Charlie ('Is this good?') makes it land harder. Visually funny moment.

jokes.text: Mac tries to sell cocaine by calling it 'nose clams fresh from the sea' — an extended, increasingly desperate metaphor that Bingo cannot decode at all
jokes.setup: Mac and Charlie need to discreetly sell drugs to a drug dealer who is himself a drug dealer and already knows what drugs are
jokes.punchline: Mac's euphemism is so bizarre ('nose clams that make you want to dance the night away') that even Bingo — who sells drugs for a living — cannot figure out what he's talking about
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best sequences. The comedic premise is layered: (1) They're trying to be subtle with someone who doesn't need subtlety, (2) the euphemism chosen is completely incomprehensible, (3) it escalates — 'clams that make you dance' → crushing into a line → snorting through a dollar bill → 'they come from Colombia' → 'they rhyme with propane.' The escalation to literal description while still maintaining the frame is superb. 'They rhyme with propane' is an all-timer. High originality because this specific comedic premise (being too discreet with a drug dealer) is fresh and perfectly executed.

jokes.text: 'They're illegal. And they rhyme with propane.' — Mac's final clue before Bingo figures out they mean cocaine
jokes.setup: Mac has exhausted every other euphemism for cocaine without Bingo understanding
jokes.punchline: 'They rhyme with propane' — the worst possible clue that is also technically correct and somehow the one that works
jokes.explanation: The best single line in the episode. After an escalating sequence of increasingly desperate hints, Mac lands on 'they rhyme with propane' — which is both utterly useless as a drug clue and technically, beautifully accurate. It's the comedic equivalent of running out of ideas and accidentally stumbling into genius. The economy is perfect (four words), the originality is exceptional (no one has ever used this clue), and the earned quality is very high because it's the culmination of a well-built sequence. This is approaching the 9.5 anchor territory.

jokes.text: Bingo: 'So you want to sell me cocaine?' Mac: 'Yes!' Bingo: 'Why didn't you just come out and say that? Instead of dancing around it. That is so tacky.'
jokes.setup: Mac has finally communicated that they want to sell cocaine through the most convoluted euphemism sequence imaginable
jokes.punchline: Bingo calls THEM tacky for being indirect — a drug dealer scolding two amateurs for not being direct enough about selling drugs
jokes.explanation: The perfect button on the nose clams sequence. Bingo's indignation — 'That is so tacky' — reframes the entire exchange. He's not threatening or confused; he's offended by their social etiquette. 'That is the kindergarten behavior of drug dealing' is a great character-specific insult. Well-structured payoff to a well-built sequence.

jokes.text: Charlie's response to Bingo's eye-contact request — looking straight up and asking 'Is this good?' while Bingo examines him
jokes.setup: Bingo tells them not to look at him, then says 'eyes, boom' after the transaction
jokes.punchline: Charlie's literal compliance — tilting his head back at a 90-degree angle, earnestly asking if this is acceptable — is a perfect visual beat
jokes.explanation: A solid visual/reaction beat. Charlie's earnest compliance with arbitrary criminal rituals is perfectly in character. Stronger as a visual moment than a quotable line.

jokes.text: Two gangsters enter; Charlie asks 'Oh shit, are you guys gangsters?' — one answers 'Shut up' — Charlie says 'Ah, owe me a Coke.'
jokes.setup: Two intimidating men walk in and confront Mac and Charlie about the drugs
jokes.punchline: Charlie's response to being told 'shut up' is to invoke the childhood game 'jinx/owe me a Coke' — treating a mob threat like a playground interaction
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's sharpest jokes. Charlie applies kindergarten social logic to a mob confrontation with zero self-awareness — the same quality that made joke 8 work, but executed more economically. 'Owe me a Coke' as a response to mob intimidation is unexpected, perfectly in character, and highly quotable. The character integration is near-perfect: this is specifically how Charlie's brain works.

jokes.text: Mac and Charlie claim to be 'six beers deep' and ask the gangster to repeat his threat more clearly
jokes.setup: The gangster has just delivered a long, incomprehensible threat
jokes.punchline: Rather than fear or compliance, Mac and Charlie's response is to explain they're drunk and ask for clarification — treating the mob threat like a confusing takeout order
jokes.explanation: The gang's complete absence of appropriate fear response is a running character trait played well here. 'I was very confused by the whole thing to be honest with you' is a good line.

jokes.text: Gangster threatens to 'chop your limbs off and distribute them evenly amongst your friends and your family' — then adds 'And that's Friday.'
jokes.setup: Mac asks what happens on Friday (the deadline to pay $25k)
jokes.punchline: The threat is cartoonishly specific in its bureaucratic precision ('distribute them evenly') followed by the absurdly casual confirmation 'And that's Friday' — as if reading from a calendar
jokes.explanation: The phrase 'distribute them evenly amongst your friends and your family' is what makes this exceptional — it's not just a violent threat, it's a logistically considerate violent threat. The bureaucratic precision of 'evenly distributed' applied to dismemberment is genuinely original dark comedy. 'And that's Friday' as a matter-of-fact calendar note seals it. This approaches the 8.0 anchor benchmark.

jokes.text: Mac and Charlie politely thank the gangsters for their clarity and promise to 'get right on that' — the gangsters say 'That's muched appreciated. Good day to youse.'
jokes.setup: Gangsters have just threatened dismemberment
jokes.punchline: Both parties exchange pleasantries as if concluding a business meeting — 'Good day to youse' — including the malapropism 'muched appreciated'
jokes.explanation: 'Muched appreciated' is a good malapropism that humanizes the gangsters in a funny way. The mutual politeness after dismemberment threats is a nice tonal note — Sunny's specialty.

jokes.text: Charlie enters singing '♪ Guess who sold the drugs / And we can fix the lights now ♪'
jokes.setup: Mac and Charlie have just been threatened by the mob; the bar still has no lights
jokes.punchline: Charlie enters with a self-congratulatory improvised victory song, oblivious to the mob problem, having solved only the smaller of the two crises
jokes.explanation: Charlie improvising a celebration song about successfully selling drugs while the gang has just been threatened with dismemberment is brilliant character work. It's pure Charlie — tone-deaf, proud, musical, oblivious. The song structure ('Guess who sold the drugs / And we can fix the lights now') is weirdly catchy and perfectly captures his childlike self-satisfaction. High character integration because only Charlie celebrates this way in this moment.

jokes.text: Dennis: 'Real-life actual gangsters. It was pretty cool.' / Mac corrects: 'It was not cool!'
jokes.setup: Dennis describes the gangsters who threatened to dismember them
jokes.punchline: Dennis characterizes a mob death threat as 'pretty cool' until Mac corrects him
jokes.explanation: Quick character beat — Dennis's reaction to meeting actual mobsters is excitement, not fear. Very Dennis. The quick Mac correction lands well but it's a minor beat.

jokes.text: Mac reveals they got $300 for $25,000 worth of cocaine — Charlie counts dramatically: 'a one, a two, a $300! Hello.'
jokes.setup: The gang needs $25,000 to pay the mob; Mac negotiated with Bingo
jokes.punchline: Charlie's theatrical countdown builds to the punchline reveal: they made $300. 'Hello.' seals it.
jokes.explanation: The dramatic countdown — 'a one, a two, a $300' — is a great performance choice that makes the disaster land harder. Charlie's triumphant 'Hello' as punctuation suggests he still thinks this is a win, which is perfect character work.

jokes.text: Mac says he was using 'Dead Presidents' as a cover — Charlie explains he told Bingo he wanted 'many, many thousands of green people from history times'
jokes.setup: Mac claims he asked for more money using slang; Dennis is confused
jokes.punchline: Charlie's literal translation of 'Dead Presidents' (dollar bill slang) reveals he described it as 'green people from history times' — which Bingo would have understood as nothing
jokes.explanation: 'Green people from history times' is an exceptional Charlie-ism. It's not just wrong — it's wrong in a specifically Charlie way that reveals exactly how his brain processes language and metaphor. The phrase is both hilarious and oddly poetic. High originality and character integration — only Charlie arrives at this translation.

jokes.text: 'We are going to get whacked off by a bunch of scary Italian guys'
jokes.setup: Dennis is explaining the seriousness of the mob threat
jokes.punchline: He uses 'whacked off' (masturbation slang) instead of 'whacked' (killed) — escalating when corrected: 'They implied they wanted to whack us all off!'
jokes.explanation: A reliable but not exceptional double entendre. Gets a laugh from the escalation ('whack us ALL off') but it's a relatively cheap joke compared to the episode's better material. Not particularly character-specific — any character could make this mistake.

jokes.text: Frank: 'Nobody's gonna get whacked off today, okay? Listen.'
jokes.setup: Mac fears they're going to 'get whacked off' by the mob
jokes.punchline: Frank earnestly reassures everyone 'nobody's gonna get whacked off today' using the same wrong phrase, as though the sexual connotation simply doesn't exist
jokes.explanation: Extension of the whacked-off gag — having Frank repeat it deadpan is a slight escalation but the joke is already spent by this point. The repetition adds some value but diminishing returns are setting in.

jokes.text: Mac tells Charlie 'Frank said to tell you to sell us back our drugs' — having been specifically told not to mention Frank's name
jokes.setup: Frank has again begged them not to mention his name when going back to Bingo
jokes.punchline: Mac immediately invokes Frank's name again — this time even more explicitly attributing the drug deal to Frank by name
jokes.explanation: A solid callback that earns its laugh by being an exact repeat of the same mistake — not a variation, the same error. Mac is constitutionally incapable of not saying Frank's name, which is funnier than if he had tried and failed.

jokes.text: Bingo offers the gang an exotic bird when they ask what they can get for $300
jokes.setup: The gang is trying to buy drugs they can flip for profit; they only have $300
jokes.punchline: Bingo offers an exotic bird — delivered completely straight, as if this is a normal part of his drug dealing inventory
jokes.explanation: The randomness of 'exotic bird' works because it's delivered as an utterly reasonable suggestion. Bingo's matter-of-fact criminal weirdness is good character work. Quick and punchy.

jokes.text: The gang can't come up with $800 each — suggestions include 'my money tree,' a leprechaun with a pot of gold, calling Donald Trump, and asking a bank if they have an account there
jokes.setup: Bingo offers OxyContin for $1,200; the gang debates whether to pool money
jokes.punchline: Their alternatives to raising $800 each escalate from vaguely plausible to completely fantastical — culminating in 'asking a bank if they have an account there'
jokes.explanation: A solid group escalation sequence. 'Do I have an account here?' is the best individual line — the idea of going to a bank as a Hail Mary and not even knowing your own account status is perfectly pathetic. Gets a bit crowded but each beat adds something.

jokes.text: The gang blames the economy — 'Have you taken a close look at the marketplace? The NASDAQ! Dow Jones! It's up then down.'
jokes.setup: Bingo asks how three men in their 30s don't have $800 between them
jokes.punchline: They pivot to blaming macroeconomic forces — the NASDAQ, Dow Jones — as if financial markets are responsible for their personal poverty, delivered with great urgency
jokes.explanation: The gang's deflection to blaming Wall Street for their inability to scrape together a few hundred dollars is a good character moment. 'It's up then down' as an economic analysis is appropriately vague and dumb. Works as a group comedy beat.

jokes.text: Mac blames the economy: 'The economy is in shambles. Have you taken a close look at the marketplace right now? The NASDAQ! Dow Jones! It's up then down.'
jokes.setup: Bingo asks why three grown men can't pool $800
jokes.punchline: Mac's explanation pivots to macroeconomic analysis — citing the NASDAQ and Dow Jones with zero specificity or relevance
jokes.explanation: 'It's up then down' as a summary of stock market analysis is a perfectly dumb Mac line. His pivot to macroeconomics to explain personal poverty is a classic gang deflection move.

jokes.text: Frank suggests the gang go into prostitution to raise mob money — Dennis is horrified — Frank clarifies he meant male escort, 'not talking about you' (Dee) because 'guys at those country clubs get hotter broads than you'
jokes.setup: Frank suggests prostitution to raise $25,000 by Friday
jokes.punchline: The double insult: (1) Dee assumes Frank means her, he clarifies he doesn't — because she's not attractive enough for the clientele. (2) The actual plan is male escort, which Frank pitches completely sincerely.
jokes.explanation: The pivot — Dee's indignation reversed into humiliation ('guys at those country clubs get hotter broads than you') — is effective. Frank's complete matter-of-fact sincerity about male escort as a business solution is perfect for his character.

jokes.text: Charlie eagerly volunteers himself as the male escort — 'I'm picking up what you're putting down. I'll do it.'
jokes.setup: Frank has proposed sending someone as a male escort to country club women
jokes.punchline: Charlie, the least suited person for this role, immediately and enthusiastically volunteers with no self-awareness
jokes.explanation: The enthusiasm of 'I'm picking up what you're putting down' followed by Frank's immediate shot-down ('Charlie, you're not quite cut from the right cloth') is a good beat. Charlie volunteering for inappropriate roles is consistent character work.

jokes.text: Frank rejects Charlie (wrong cloth), then Mac (too low class, women will think they'll 'catch something from him') — lands on Dennis, who asks if the women will be attractive. Told 'probably not' — 'Then I'm not going to do it. Let's sell some drugs.'
jokes.setup: Frank is auditioning the gang for the male escort role
jokes.punchline: Dennis's vain conditions (must be attractive women) are his dealbreaker — he'd rather face the mob than sleep with unattractive women
jokes.explanation: Dennis's vanity/narcissism is one of his defining character traits, and this sequence exploits it perfectly. The escalating rejections (Charlie/Mac) build to Dennis, who would be the best choice — but his condition ('will any of them be attractive?') and instant rejection reveal his narcissism is stronger than his survival instinct. 'Then I'm not going to do it. Let's sell some drugs.' is a great line.

jokes.text: Frank rejects Charlie for the escort role: 'Charlie, you're not quite cut from the right cloth.'
jokes.setup: Charlie eagerly volunteers to be a male escort
jokes.punchline: Frank's diplomatic rejection implies Charlie is too low-class, gross, or simply not escort material — without elaborating
jokes.explanation: A quick character beat. The implication that Charlie's grossness makes him ineligible even for prostitution is consistent with the show's treatment of his character. The vagueness of 'right cloth' is funnier than a specific reason would be.

jokes.text: Frank starts coaching Dee to play his secretary 'Linda,' insisting she not have opinions because 'these guys are old school, they don't like women's rights'
jokes.setup: Frank and Dee are playing roles to infiltrate the country club — Frank as executive, Dee as secretary
jokes.punchline: Frank's coaching reveals he's completely sincere about the gender dynamics, treating 1950s sexism as practical business advice
jokes.explanation: Setup for the subsequent Dee vs. Frank bit. Frank's sexism is in character but not particularly surprising. Functions mainly as scene establishment.

jokes.text: Frank tells Dennis: 'You're already a whore. Why not make some money at it?' and Dennis responds by worrying Frank is planning to escalate him from old ladies to dudes
jokes.setup: Frank tries to convince Dennis to be an escort
jokes.punchline: Frank dismisses Dennis's self-image with 'You're already a whore' — and Dennis's worry is a very specific escalation fear: 'You're gonna have me move on to dudes'
jokes.explanation: Dennis's specific fear trajectory — old ladies → dudes — reveals both his homophobia and his resigned acceptance that Frank will escalate things. Frank's 'You're already a whore' is a devastating character assessment. Good character integration.

jokes.text: Charlie encounters the horse trainer, is told the last stable boy had his 'brains kicked in' by the horse and 'takes his food through a straw now' — Charlie responds 'I bet. Hey, you wouldn't be interested in taking his job, would ya?'
jokes.setup: Charlie has been enchanted by the horse and the trainer notes the horse 'normally doesn't take to strangers'
jokes.punchline: The trainer casually mentions the previous employee's catastrophic brain injury as context — then immediately offers Charlie the same job. Charlie accepts.
jokes.explanation: Dark and efficient — the brain injury is disclosed not as a warning but as a fun anecdote, immediately followed by a job offer. Charlie's acceptance without hesitation is perfect. 'Takes his food through a straw now. I bet.' is a great exchange — Charlie's casual acknowledgment of horrific information is very in character.

jokes.text: Charlie is surprised the jockey can talk: 'Holy shit. You can talk? That is great. I would've figured if anything, your voice would be like super high.'
jokes.setup: Charlie meets an actual horse jockey who speaks to him
jokes.punchline: Charlie expresses genuine shock that the jockey is capable of speech, then reveals he expected a high voice — treating the jockey as essentially non-human
jokes.explanation: Charlie's species-level misunderstanding of jockeys is perfect character comedy. The specific detail of expecting a high voice — as though small size automatically correlates with vocal pitch — reveals Charlie's deep ignorance without malice. The cringe comes from Charlie's sincerity.

jokes.text: Trainer asks if Charlie has 'any qualms about picking up shit' — Charlie accepts enthusiastically — Trainer: 'Usually we'd use a shovel for that. But to each his own.'
jokes.setup: Charlie is being interviewed for the stable hand job
jokes.punchline: Charlie's enthusiasm for picking up horse excrement (implied to be barehanded) is so apparent that the trainer notes the shovel is optional — 'to each his own'
jokes.explanation: 'To each his own' about barehanded fecal collection is very funny deadpan. The implication — that Charlie's enthusiasm for the job is somehow more than even a stable hand requires — is excellent. High character integration because Charlie's relationship with filth and low-status work is a core character trait.

jokes.text: Frank and Dee's elaborate business role-play — Frank insisting on being called 'Bob' while ordering Dee (as 'Linda') around, complete with fabricated phone calls to 'Jameson'
jokes.setup: Frank and Dee need to seem like high-powered executives to sell drugs at a country club
jokes.punchline: Frank commits FULLY to this elaborate character bit in a public space, complete with names, phone calls, and fictional investment amounts — Dee increasingly reluctant
jokes.explanation: Setup joke for the stronger payoffs (joke 35, joke 36). Functional cringe but not exceptional on its own.

jokes.text: Dee subverts Frank's executive role-play — when he asks her to call Jameson about $650K investment, she asks 'How about you do it?' and gradually dismantles his authority by asking what they're investing in — 'Lasers. Lasers!' — Dee: 'That is adorable.'
jokes.setup: Frank is performing as a powerful executive with Dee as his subservient secretary 'Linda'
jokes.punchline: Dee's systematic deconstruction of Frank's business authority exposes that his 'investment' is 'Lasers' — delivered with the confidence of a visionary and shot down by Dee's perfectly timed 'That is adorable'
jokes.explanation: 'Lasers!' delivered as a business visionary's answer, followed by 'That is adorable' as Dee's quiet kill-shot, is very good. The structure of the scene — Dee slowly dismantling Frank's authority with simple questions — is well-constructed. 'Lasers. Lasers!' with its escalating repetition is the comedic peak.

jokes.text: Mac's 'Bob' character calls Jameson to reject a $650,000 investment: 'Tell him I don't need his $650,000 investment. He can shove it right back up his ass.'
jokes.setup: Mac is performing the role of a high-powered executive to impress country club members
jokes.punchline: Mac's executive persona is so committed that he's making up phone calls to fake clients, turning down fake millions — all while trying to sell stolen OxyContin
jokes.explanation: Mac's delusion-of-grandeur performance is a decent bit. The specific dollar amount and the 'shove it right back up his ass' makes the fake power trip funnier. Supporting beat to the Mac-Dee exchange.

jokes.text: Dee turns the tables on Mac: she tells 'Bob' to call Jameson himself, then challenges him on what Jameson is investing in. Mac says 'lasers.' Dee says 'Adorable.'
jokes.setup: Mac has set Dee up as his subservient secretary 'Linda'; Dee immediately starts undermining the bit
jokes.punchline: When pressed on the substance of his fictional deal, Mac can only say 'lasers' — exposing the total hollowness of his executive persona. Dee's 'adorable' is devastating.
jokes.explanation: One of the strongest jokes in the episode. The comedic structure is elegant: Mac builds an elaborate fake persona, Dee systematically dismantles it with reasonable questions, and Mac's one-word answer ('Lasers!') perfectly encapsulates the total emptiness of his grandiosity. 'Adorable' from Dee lands as one of the best Dee lines in the episode. The 'Lasers!' repetition is also funny — Mac doubling down rather than elaborating.

jokes.text: Dee, done with the ruse, turns to random country club members and says flatly: 'Who wants to buy some drugs?'
jokes.setup: Frank and Dee have been doing an elaborate business executive role-play to sell drugs subtly
jokes.punchline: Dee abandons all pretense and directly propositions strangers in a country club for drug sales
jokes.explanation: Perfect economy — five words that demolish an entire elaborate preceding setup. After the nose clams sequence where Mac was TOO indirect, Dee is completely direct at the worst possible moment. The structural contrast with joke 13 makes this land even harder. 'Who wants to buy some drugs?' at a country club is a great button — sharp, quotable, and perfectly timed.

jokes.text: A gigolo recruiter approaches Dennis: 'Don't play dumb with me, hermano. I know a gigolo when I see one.'
jokes.setup: Dennis is wandering the country club, refusing to be Frank's whore
jokes.punchline: He's immediately clocked as gigolo material by a professional — confirming Frank's assessment while Dennis is still insisting he won't be a 'whore'
jokes.explanation: 'I know a gigolo when I see one' is good because it validates Dennis's attractiveness while also being deeply humiliating. 'Hermano' is a nice character touch for the recruiter. Sets up Dennis's escort subplot.

jokes.text: The pimp corrects Dennis's assumption: 'Bang them? No, bro. You got it all wrong, man. These women are classy. They just want someone to be nice to them. Flirt a little bit. That's it.'
jokes.setup: Dennis is horrified at the idea of 'banging old ladies'
jokes.punchline: The pimp reveals it's actually just companionship — fancy dinners, exotic vacations — subverting Dennis's (and the audience's) expectation that this is a sex work proposition
jokes.explanation: Good misdirection — the audience (and Dennis) has been expecting this to be a straight prostitution pitch, so the revelation that it's actually just companions flipping the expectation is satisfying. Sets up Dennis's full arc into the escort lifestyle.

jokes.text: Dennis receives $20 from the gigolo handler — only gets $20 out of whatever the client paid — handler says 'Take it or leave it.' Dennis takes it. Handler walks off muttering 'Puta pendejo.'
jokes.setup: Dennis has been sold on the glamorous escort lifestyle
jokes.punchline: He gets paid $20 and immediately accepts it — the recruiter insults him in Spanish as he walks away — Dennis doesn't understand/react
jokes.explanation: The gap between the promised glamour and the $20 reality is a solid gag. 'Puta pendejo' as a departing insult Dennis can't understand is a nice touch — the recruiter's contempt for Dennis mirrors the audience's.

jokes.text: Charlie declares 'Nobody parties like a jockey!' after selling all his pills to horse jockeys
jokes.setup: Charlie has wandered away from the drug-selling plan to work at the stables
jokes.punchline: He's accidentally sold all his OxyContin to tiny horse jockeys, delivering the verdict 'Nobody parties like a jockey!' as established folk wisdom
jokes.explanation: 'Nobody parties like a jockey!' is a great line — it's delivered as if this is universally known wisdom, the specificity of jockeys as drug enthusiasts is unexpected, and it's exactly the conclusion Charlie's chaotic adventure would reach. High quotability and economy.

jokes.text: Charlie responds to 'nobody parties like a jockey' by saying 'I was not familiar with that expression, Buster. I didn't even know you guys could talk.'
jokes.setup: Buster (the horse trainer) has just said the jockey party line
jokes.punchline: Charlie, in complete sincerity, says he didn't know the jockeys 'could talk' — either mistaking them for the horses he's been bonding with, or genuinely surprised by jockeys' sentience
jokes.explanation: Exceptional Charlie-ism. 'I didn't even know you guys could talk' — said earnestly about fully grown adult humans who are jockeys — is a window into Charlie's profoundly strange interior world. It's ambiguous whether he's comparing them to the horse he's bonded with or genuinely confused about jockeys. Either reading is funnier than the other. High character integration.

jokes.text: Charlie: 'I was not familiar with that expression, Buster. I didn't even know you guys could talk.'
jokes.setup: Buster delivers the 'nobody parties like a jockey' proverb
jokes.punchline: Charlie (1) has never heard this fake saying, and (2) casually reveals he STILL doesn't believe jockeys can speak — despite having just spoken with one at length
jokes.explanation: Perfect callback to Charlie's earlier shock at jockey speech. The fact that Charlie still frames jockey speech as the exceptional condition — 'I didn't even know you guys could talk' — after a full conversation with one is a great escalation of his fundamental weirdness. High character integration.

jokes.text: Charlie tells the horse trainer he has 'a little something to straighten out with the mafia' before potentially taking the stable job — 'You know how that goes, right?' Trainer: 'Oh, sure.'
jokes.setup: Trainer offers Charlie the stable hand job
jokes.punchline: Charlie casually mentions needing to resolve a mafia situation first — delivered as the most ordinary logistical hurdle — and the trainer accepts this completely
jokes.explanation: The mutual casual acceptance of mob involvement as a normal scheduling conflict is perfectly executed. 'Oh, sure' from the trainer — not shocked, just accommodating — is the right response.

jokes.text: Charlie believes he was a centaur in a past life because of eye contact with the horse
jokes.setup: Charlie is bonding with the horse and reflecting on the connection
jokes.punchline: He concludes from sustained eye contact that he was 'half-man, half-horse' in a past life — delivered with complete spiritual sincerity
jokes.explanation: Charlie's mystical connection to animals leading to a past-life centaur theory is exactly the kind of sincere, internally-logical nonsense Charlie specializes in. The trainer's response ('something tells me you probably were never half-man, half-horse') is excellent measured understatement.

jokes.text: Buster responds: 'Well, something tells me you probably were never half-man, half-horse. But hell, what do I know? All I know is you got a great attitude.'
jokes.setup: Charlie seriously proposes he was a centaur in a past life
jokes.punchline: Buster gently disputes the centaur claim but then pivots to praising Charlie's attitude — as though 'great attitude' is the relevant takeaway from the centaur revelation
jokes.explanation: Good deadpan response. Buster's diplomatic handling of the centaur claim — a soft 'probably not' followed by a redirect — is a perfect straight man beat. The pivot to 'great attitude' as though that's the most important outcome of the centaur conversation is quietly very funny.

jokes.text: Horse trainer Buster: 'Come on, you old son of a gun, and let Buster do a line off your boner.' — pause — Charlie: 'No?'
jokes.setup: Buster has been a folksy, warm horse trainer — Charlie's potential mentor figure — giving a touching speech about attitude
jokes.punchline: Buster pivots abruptly to asking to do cocaine off Charlie's erection — Charlie's 'No?' suggests this is somehow a question, not a refusal
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes and among the more shocking non-sequiturs in the show's history. The setup is a warm, mentor-student moment about attitude and horses — Buster sounds like a loveable character. Then: 'let Buster do a line off your boner.' The specificity, the casual familiarity ('you old son of a gun'), the third-person self-reference ('Buster'), and the implied cocaine all compound into something genuinely surprising. Charlie's 'No?' — questioning rather than refusing — suggests he's not even certain of his own answer. This is exceptional dark comedy writing.

jokes.text: Dennis tries to order a 'strawberry daiquiri' by calling the waiter 'garzon' (mangled French for garçon), affecting a ridiculous accent
jokes.setup: Dennis is performing his escort role at the country club bar
jokes.punchline: His attempt at continental sophistication ('garzon') immediately reveals he doesn't actually know French, undermining his glamorous facade
jokes.explanation: A quick character beat — Dennis's sophisticated self-image undercut by basic linguistic failure. Functional but minor.

jokes.text: Charlie interrupts Dennis's escort hustle smelling of horse manure — insists it's cheese because 'the horse was eating a lot of cheese'
jokes.setup: Dennis is mid-seduction at the bar when Charlie arrives covered in stable filth
jokes.punchline: Charlie insists the smell is cheese (not horse excrement) because 'the horse was eating a lot of cheese' — a completely impossible explanation delivered with absolute conviction
jokes.explanation: Charlie's unwillingness to admit it's horse shit — even as Dennis directly names it — is good stubborn character comedy. 'The horse was eating a lot of cheese' is the kind of unverifiable deflection only Charlie would use.

jokes.text: Frank declares 'I am your pimp. You are my ho.' to Dennis in public
jokes.setup: Dee is trying to tell Frank to stop embarrassing Dennis in front of a potential client
jokes.punchline: Frank clarifies the power structure by stating plainly that he is Dennis's pimp and Dennis is his prostitute — in a country club
jokes.explanation: Very economical — Frank's bluntness is his defining quality and 'I am your pimp, you are my ho' captures it perfectly in a maximally inappropriate social context. Good line.

jokes.text: Frank tells Dennis: 'Don't talk to me that way. Don't talk to me. I am your pimp. You are my ho.'
jokes.setup: Dennis tells Frank to leave the escort setup because he smells bad
jokes.punchline: Frank asserts his authority by declaring himself Dennis's pimp and Dennis his ho — apparently this dynamic has already been established between them
jokes.explanation: Frank's matter-of-fact assertion of the pimp/ho hierarchy with Dennis is a good character beat. The authority claim is funny precisely because Frank has zero social awareness that this is an absurd thing to say publicly.

jokes.text: Security escorts Mac and Frank off the country club property; Mac is told he 'made a whole series of bad decisions'
jokes.setup: The gang has been trying to sell drugs at a country club
jokes.punchline: Mac's unnamed 'series of bad decisions' is funnier for being unspecified — we don't know what specifically happened, implying it was too much to enumerate
jokes.explanation: Light scene transition joke. 'A whole series of bad decisions' is funny for its vagueness but isn't exceptional.

jokes.text: Dennis: 'I will be providing a very important service, however, as what I would like to be called a handsome companion.' Frank: 'To dudes?' Dennis: 'No, not to dudes.'
jokes.setup: Frank declares 'Dennis is a prostitute now'
jokes.punchline: Dennis insists on the euphemism 'handsome companion' and vehemently clarifies it's not for men — his main concern being the gender of his clientele rather than the ethics of the arrangement
jokes.explanation: 'Handsome companion' is a perfect Dennis euphemism — it captures his narcissism and his need to maintain self-image. His vehement 'not to dudes' as the principal objection tells us everything about his character. Good character integration.

jokes.text: Mac declares himself 'boss' and starts directing everyone — the gang unanimously rejects his authority and physically abandons him at the country club, telling him to 'walk like the rest of the Americans'
jokes.setup: Mac has been increasingly assertive about being 'the boss'; the gang has been dismissing him
jokes.punchline: The gang leaves him behind at the country club 40 miles away — his response is to yell 'I'm smart and I deserve respect!' as they drive off
jokes.explanation: 'Walk like the rest of the Americans' is a great dismissal — weirdly patriotic and maximally unhelpful. Mac screaming 'I'm smart and I deserve respect!' while being abandoned is good character work. The gang's casual cruelty is the show's signature.

jokes.text: Mac left at the country club: 'How am I supposed to get home?' Dee: 'You're supposed to walk like the rest of the Americans. You walk, you know? On their two feet!' Mac: 'Walk? It's like 40 miles!'
jokes.setup: The gang is kicking Mac out of the operation for being bossy; they're leaving him at the country club
jokes.punchline: Dee tells him to walk home 'like the rest of the Americans' with patriotic gravity — and Mac is horrified because it's 40 miles
jokes.explanation: 'Walk like the rest of the Americans' as a patriotic framing for abandoning someone is a funny Dee choice. Mac's '40 miles!' adds appropriate scale of absurdity.

jokes.text: Mac nearly runs the gangsters over with his car — 'I put the parking brake on. Sorry about that, boys.'
jokes.setup: Mac has been abandoned and is apparently now driving — he nearly hits the gangsters who are waiting for their money
jokes.punchline: Mac's apology for nearly killing them is casual and brief — 'Sorry about that, boys' — as if he nearly knocked over a parking meter
jokes.explanation: Good physical comedy beat — the nonchalance of the apology for nearly vehicular-manslaughtering mob enforcers is in keeping with the gang's total inability to process danger appropriately.

jokes.text: Frank attempts to tell the gangsters he 'may or may not have had absolutely nothing to do with it' — they point out 'you just said you did have something to do with it' — the double negative debate
jokes.setup: Frank is trying to distance himself from the drug situation using careful hedging language — mirroring the gangsters' own obfuscation from earlier
jokes.punchline: Frank's double negative collapses under interrogation — 'I did have absolutely nothing' becomes 'you did have something' — and Frank can't escape his own grammar
jokes.explanation: A structural callback — Frank tries to use the same hedging language the gangsters used, and it immediately backfires. The double negative grammar trap is legitimately clever and the gangsters' patient correction ('that's what I heard') is a nice role reversal.

jokes.text: Frank tells the gangsters he wants to 'dress like a track star, wear gold shit and slick my hair back and grow a pompadour' and join their crew
jokes.setup: Frank is supposed to be explaining why he isn't responsible for the drug situation
jokes.punchline: Instead he pivots to confessing that he's always wanted to be in the mob for the aesthetic — the tracksuit, the pompadour — with the earnestness of a child admitting a dream
jokes.explanation: Frank's sincere desire to be a mob associate because of the fashion choices is perfect Frank energy — corrupt, childlike, completely tone-deaf to the danger of the moment. 'Gold shit and slick my hair back' is a good line. Very high character integration.

jokes.text: The gangsters make Frank their 'bitch' — have him clean their bathrooms as the first step to joining the crew
jokes.setup: Frank earnestly wants to prove his loyalty to the mob
jokes.punchline: His first task toward becoming a mobster is cleaning bathrooms — the gangsters plan to use him as labor until Friday, then 'whack him off irregardless'
jokes.explanation: Frank's humiliation — a wealthy businessman cleaning mob bathrooms — is well-earned. His complete lack of suspicion makes it funnier.

jokes.text: Frank mentions he learned to clean bathrooms from his friend Charlie — 'You'll get to know him too maybe.' Gangster: 'I'm sure you will.'
jokes.setup: Frank is enthusiastically taking on the bathroom-cleaning role as a path to mob membership
jokes.punchline: The gangster's knowing 'I'm sure you will' — implying they'll get Charlie too, as the gang is all equally doomed — is a dark understated threat
jokes.explanation: A quiet dark beat — the gangster's knowing comment implies the whole gang's doom without spelling it out. Good economy.

jokes.text: The mob boss reveals their real plan: 'Hey, summer squash for brains, I'm gonna make him our bitch till Friday. And after that? I wanna whack him off irregardless.'
jokes.setup: The other gangster asks if they're really letting Frank join the crew
jokes.punchline: The boss reveals the plan: (1) Frank is a 'bitch boy' until Friday, then (2) they'll 'whack him off irregardless' — using the wrong word twice (irregardless instead of regardless, and the whacked-off double-entendre callback)
jokes.explanation: The final joke of the episode lands multiple callbacks simultaneously: (1) 'summer squash for brains' as a mob insult is a funny original detail, (2) 'whack him off irregardless' callbacks the episode's 'whacked off' running gag AND adds 'irregardless' (a famously wrong word) as an additional language joke, mirroring the grammar correction earlier. The mob boss who corrected Frank's double negative now uses 'irregardless' — a great internal irony. Strong episode ender.

jokes.text: Gangster 1 tells Gangster 2 the plan is to use Frank as a 'bitch boy' until Friday — 'And after that? I wanna whack him off irregardless.'
jokes.setup: The gangsters privately discuss their plan for Frank
jokes.punchline: 'Whack him off' (echoing Dennis's earlier malapropism) + 'irregardless' (a malapropism for 'regardless') in the same sentence — the gangster who's been threatening dismemberment is also grammatically confused
jokes.explanation: The episode closes on a callback to Dennis's 'whacked off' joke — but now delivered by the actual gangster, making it more absurd. 'Irregardless' as a final-line malapropism from a mob enforcer is a perfect button for the episode: these threatening villains are just as linguistically confused as the gang. Very economical and satisfying callback structure for a part-one finale.

tmdb_overview: After stumbling upon a kilo of cocaine, the gang is forced to pay off a $25,000 debt to the mob. Mac becomes a mob informant, while Frank pimps out Dennis as an escort at the local country club. Charlie stumbles upon an opportunity to sell illegal narcotics.
